# Session 8 · Publish: polish your Results, get it out, present

## Week 8 · Saturday, 19:30-22:30 (online)

- 19:30  Recap: Session 7
- 19:35  8.1  Writing the paper (II): Introduction, Discussion, abstract, title
- 20:05  Manuscript workshop 2: improve your Results section
- 20:30  8.2  Getting published: from checklist to reviewers
- 21:05  8.3  Be the reviewer: Papers 1 and 2, as a whole class
- 21:30  Proposal presentations (about 5 volunteers), 22:15 closing

::: {.notes}
Session 8 (19:30-22:30, break 20:50-21:05). The last session.

Today: the Introduction, Discussion, abstract and title, improving the Results drafts, publishing, reviewing, and about five proposal presentations. The closing (22:15) has its own slides.

Before: email the exercise sheet and the original papers. Remind everyone to bring their own Results draft and the results pack for their question. Collect and open the presenters' slides.
:::

## Recap: three questions from Session 7

::: {.neu-banner style="--c:#6C3483"}
QUICK QUIZ · 5 min
:::

::: {.neu-activity-steps style="--c:#6C3483"}
- Who consents for a sedated patient in septic shock?
- Which STROBE item asks for crude and adjusted estimates?
- Where does 'this may be because sicker patients got more fluid' belong?
:::

::: {.neu-output style="--c:#6C3483"}
**OUTPUT** Work alone (2 min): answer the three questions, then vote in the poll
:::

::: {.notes}
Recap (19:30-19:35). 2 minutes: everyone answers alone. Then one poll per question. Show the results, then the next slide. Question 1 was the exit question of Session 7: call on two or three people to read their answer.
:::

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:3"}

- The patient cannot consent
- Or deferred consent, if the ethics committee approved it
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0B376C"}
[STROBE item 16]{.neu-card-title}

- Main results
- Crude and adjusted estimates with their CIs
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#5FA39B"}
[Discussion]{.neu-card-title}

- The sentence explains a finding
- It does not report one
:::
::::

:::

Question 3 leads into 8.1: the Discussion is where interpretation lives.

Timing: within the 5 minutes of the recap.

## 8.1  \|  30 minutes

:::: {.neu-statement}
::: {.neu-big}
Writing the paper (II): Introduction, Discussion, abstract and title
:::

::: {.neu-sub}
What each part does, a worked example on Q1, a short check
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Section 8.1 (19:35-20:05). About 2 minutes per slide and three 2-minute checks.

All four parts are taught as core. For the assignment, the title is required with the Results. The Introduction, Discussion and abstract are optional to submit. Slow down on the Discussion example.
:::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Known, unknown, aim. The aim matches the primary outcome.
:::

::: {.notes}
The Introduction is a funnel: known, not known, aim. The aim matches the primary outcome.

Paper 1 does this in under 500 words. Paper 2 cites both sides of a conflict in paragraph 2.

Ask: in one sentence, what is not known about your question? That is paragraph 2.
:::

## Worked example: the Introduction funnel for FLUID-ICU (Q1)

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:3"}
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0D7377"}
[1  Known]{.neu-card-title}

- Fluids save lives early in sepsis
- A positive balance is linked to death (Paper 2 and other cohorts)
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0B376C"}
[2  Not known]{.neu-card-title}

- Sicker patients get more fluid
- Unclear whether the link remains after adjusting for severity
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#5FA39B"}
[3  Aim]{.neu-card-title}

- We examined whether a positive balance by day 3 is associated with 28-day mortality, after adjustment
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Three paragraphs, about 350 words. The aim uses 'associated'.
:::

::: {.notes}
Worked example for Q1. Model sentences (adapt, do not copy):

P2: 'Because sicker patients receive more fluid, it remains uncertain whether this association persists after adjustment for severity.'

P3: 'We therefore examined whether a positive fluid balance by day 3 was associated with 28-day mortality.'

The gap is the confounding by indication from Session 4.
:::

## Check: known, not known or aim?

::: {.neu-banner style="--c:#6C3483"}
QUICK QUIZ · 2 min
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}
::: {.neu-activity-steps style="--c:#6C3483"}
- 'Early fluids are a core part of sepsis care.'
- 'Sicker patients receive more fluid, so it is unclear whether the link with death remains after adjustment.'
- 'We examined whether a positive balance by day 3 was associated with 28-day mortality.'
- 'In our cohort, 35.9% of patients with a positive balance died.'
:::
:::
::: {.column width="40%"}
::: {.neu-side .plain style="--c:#6C3483"}
Choose

- Known
- Not known
- Aim
- Not in the Introduction
:::
:::
::::

::: {.neu-output style="--c:#6C3483"}
**OUTPUT** Work alone (1 min): label each sentence, then vote in the poll
:::

::: {.notes}
Check (2 minutes). 1 minute alone, then one poll per sentence. Call on one or two people to explain sentence 4. Answers on the next slide.
:::

## Answers: known, not known or aim?

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:4"}
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0D7377"}
[Known]{.neu-card-title}

- Paragraph 1
- Established practice
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0B376C"}
[Not known]{.neu-card-title}

- Paragraph 2
- It names the gap
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#5FA39B"}
[Aim]{.neu-card-title}

- Paragraph 3
- It states what we examined
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0070C0"}
[Not in the Introduction]{.neu-card-title}

- Our own result
- It goes in the Results
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** The Introduction never reports your own results.
:::

::: {.notes}
Sentence 4 is the trap.

Timing: within the 2 minutes of the check.
:::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Answer first. Limitations with their direction. Conclusion = abstract = title.
:::

::: {.notes}
The picture shows six cards, one per move, in the order you write them. Each card says what the move does (bold) and gives an example from Paper 1 or Paper 2 (green = good practice, red = a weak point).

Compare and Explain are different jobs. Compare looks outward: do other studies find the same direction and size? Explain looks inward: why might we have found this (mechanism, bias or confounding)?

The Conclusion is not a summary of the numbers. It answers the research question in one take-home sentence, with the same message as the abstract and title.

Paper 1 answers in its first Discussion sentence (p.8) and names control-group contamination as a limitation, with a fix. Its 'would probably be advantageous' is speculation without data.

Poll: which move do first-time writers skip? Expected: the direction of each limitation.
:::

::: {.notes}
The picture shows the six moves from the previous slide, one sentence each, in the same colours. Simulated data from results pack Q1.

1 Answer: the adjusted OR from Table 3 of the pack. 2 Compare: Paper 2, which we read in Sessions 6 and 7 (HR 2.13 on day 2). 3 Explain: Table 1 shows the positive-balance group was sicker (median SOFA 8 vs 6), and the OR fell from 2.49 to 1.62: confounding by indication. 4 Limitations: pack section 8, with the direction (the association may be overestimated) and the check (multiple imputation, OR 1.70, Table 6). 5 Implications: pack section 7. 6 Conclusion: the answer to the research question in one sentence, with no new numbers.

Ask: which pack section did each sentence come from? Nothing here is new to someone who has read the pack.

Optional for Q1 writers: the association looked stronger in heart failure (p for interaction 0.031, but few patients had heart failure). Call it a hypothesis.
:::

The forest plot shows the three odds ratios from Table 6 of results pack Q1, on a log scale with the null line at 1: crude (grey), adjusted complete-case (teal) and adjusted after multiple imputation (light teal).

Crude 2.49, adjusted 1.62, multiple imputation 1.70. The drop is the Session 4 lesson made visible.

The adjusted CI starts at 1.02: 'a modest association remained'.

Ask: what if the adjusted CI had crossed 1? Expected: 'no clear evidence of an association after adjustment', not 'no effect'.

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Climb the ladder only as far as your design allows.
:::

::: {.notes}
The picture is a ladder of verbs: the strongest claims at the top, each rung pointing to the design it needs. The red panel on the right lists four wordings never to use.

The strength of a verb is a claim. Read the ladder from the bottom.

Never: 'trend' for p = 0.42 (Paper 1), 'impact' in a cohort (Paper 2), 'first' or 'novel' unchecked.

These words matter in the Results section too.

Ask: rewrite 'positive fluid balance increases mortality' for Paper 2.
:::

## Check: fix the verb (FLUID-ICU, simulated)

::: {.neu-banner style="--c:#6C3483"}
QUICK QUIZ · 2 min
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}
::: {.neu-activity-steps style="--c:#6C3483"}
- 'A positive balance caused higher mortality (OR 1.62).'
- 'Fluid overload increases AKI (acute kidney injury) (OR 1.27 per 10 ml/kg).'
- 'There was a trend towards death (Cox HR 1.46, 95% CI 1.00 to 2.13).'
- 'Lactate predicts death (OR 1.39 per mmol/L).'
:::
:::
::: {.column width="40%"}
::: {.neu-side .plain style="--c:#6C3483"}
Choose

- Fine
- Fix
:::
:::
::::

::: {.neu-output style="--c:#6C3483"}
**OUTPUT** Work alone (1 min): write the fix, then vote 'fine' or 'fix' in the poll
:::

::: {.notes}
Check (2 minutes). 1 minute alone, then one poll per sentence. Call on two or three people for the fix. Fixes on the next slide.
:::

## Answers: fix the verb

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:4"}
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0D7377"}
[Sentence 1: fix]{.neu-card-title}

- 'was associated with higher mortality'
- A cohort cannot show cause
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0B376C"}
[Sentence 2: fix]{.neu-card-title}

- 'was associated with higher odds of AKI'
- Same reason: a cohort
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#5FA39B"}
[Sentence 3: fix]{.neu-card-title}

- No 'trend'. Give HR 1.46 (1.00 to 2.13)
- Say the CI reaches 1
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0070C0"}
[Sentence 4: fine]{.neu-card-title}

- Fine for prediction
- For a claim about cause, use 'associated with'
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** In a cohort, the verb is 'associated with'.
:::

::: {.notes}
Ask the class for the fix before you show it.

Timing: within the 2 minutes of the check.
:::

::: {.notes}
The picture shows the four sections of a structured abstract (coloured labels), what each must say (outlined boxes), and a good example from our two papers (green ticks). Top right: the length and the two rules. Bottom, in red: an error to avoid.

250-300 words, and it must stand alone, so write every term in full: no abbreviations. Trials add the registration number.

Paper 2 gives every result as a hazard ratio with its CI. Paper 1 states its negative result plainly.

Write the abstract last and check every number matches the text and tables.

Ask: what is the first thing you look for in an abstract's Results? Expected: the main effect with its confidence interval.
:::

::: {.notes}
The picture shows a complete structured abstract for Q1, written as it would appear in a journal: the title in the dark bar, then Background, Methods, Results and Conclusions (about 220 words).

Every number comes from results pack Q1: 620 enrolled, 618 analysed, 373 (60.4%) positive, 134/373 vs 45/245 deaths, crude and adjusted odds ratios.

Point out the rules: no abbreviations (odds ratio and confidence interval written in full), full sentences rather than lists, the design in the title, and 'modestly associated' to match a confidence interval of 1.02 to 2.59.

The title is required for everyone. The abstract is optional to submit, but everyone should be able to write one. In the assignment, state that the data are simulated, as the brief asks.

Ask: which sentences change if the confidence interval had been 0.95 to 2.40? Expected: Results and Conclusions ('no clear evidence of an association after adjustment').
:::

The picture shows the title formula from the PICO as four chips (design, I vs C, in P, on O), then each paper's published title (red cross) with a better version (green tick) and the problem in red. The bottom bar gives the rule for keywords.

Build the title from the PICO: 10-16 words, design stated. No 'impact', 'novel', 'first'.

Paper 1: over 25 words and value words. Paper 2: 'Impact' is causal wording for a cohort.

Keywords: 3-6 MeSH terms (PubMed subject headings) not already in the title, so the paper is found by more searches.

Everyone checks their own working title in the workshop that follows.

- Check every citation

:::

[Reporting checklist]{.neu-card-title}

- Fill it in while you write

- FLUID-ICU and Paper 2: STROBE
:::

[Final read]{.neu-card-title}

- Each 'Figure 1, 2...' in the text points to the right figure
- A colleague reads the tables
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Checking the text against the tables would have caught most errors in Papers 1 and 2.
:::

::: {.notes}
Three cards: references, the reporting checklist and the final read.

References: use a reference manager and check every citation. Never cite a reference an AI suggested without reading it.

Checklist: fill in STROBE while you write, with page numbers, as you learnt in Session 7. Neither paper names its reporting guideline. Paper 1 is a trial, and trials have their own checklist (CONSORT): 8.2 shows which checklist fits which design.

Final read: every number in the text against the tables, and every figure call-out (Paper 1 refers to Figure 1 where it means Figure 2A). These errors needed no new data, only a co-author who read the text against the tables.
:::

## Manuscript workshop 2: improve your own Results section

::: {.neu-banner style="--c:#0B376C"}
INDIVIDUAL TASK · 25 min
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}
::: {.neu-activity-steps style="--c:#0B376C"}
- Numbers: every number matches your pack, with denominators and 95% CIs
- Complete: every result in your pack is reported, in STROBE order (items 13 to 17)
- Tables and figure: each stands alone (title, units, n, abbreviations)
- Words: past tense, 'associated with', no interpretation
- Working title: population, exposure, outcome and design
:::
:::
::: {.column width="40%"}
::: {.neu-side .plain style="--c:#0B376C"}
Watch for, in your question

- Q1: crude, adjusted, Cox and multiple imputation estimates
- Q2: odds ratio per 10 ml/kg, crude and adjusted
- Q3: death counts as zero ventilator-free days
- Q4: complete-case and multiple imputation estimates
- Q5: survivors only, so say who is excluded
:::
:::
::::

::: {.neu-output style="--c:#0B376C"}
**OUTPUT** Work alone (18 min): fix your own Results section, then share one fix in the chat
:::

::: {.notes}
The slide lists five checks on the left, in the order of the Results checklist, and one point to watch for each question on the right.

Timing (20:05-20:30): 18 minutes alone, one check after another. Then 7 minutes: call on one person per question (Q1 to Q5) to read one sentence they fixed or their working title, and comment.

Prompts while they work: 'Does every percentage have a denominator?' 'Is every result in your pack in your text or a table?' 'Can Table 1 be read without the text?' 'Is any sentence explaining rather than reporting?'

Instructions: s8\_exercises Part B. Model text: s8\_solutions Part B.

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Name your guideline in Proposal Part 4 and use it as a writing checklist.
:::

::: {.notes}
The picture links each study design (outlined boxes) to its reporting guideline (filled boxes), with our examples beside CONSORT and STROBE. The dark panel on the right is the EQUATOR Network, where all checklists are free.

One reporting guideline per design, all free on the EQUATOR Network. Many journals require the checklist with page numbers.

Neither paper names its guideline.

Poll: which guideline fits your proposal? Expected: mostly STROBE.
:::

## Choosing a journal: four checks

::: {.neu-intro}
Decide the target journal before you write: it sets the rules.
:::

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:4"}
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0D7377"}
[Fit]{.neu-card-title}

- Who needs your result?
- Read 3 recent issues
- Similar designs published?
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0B376C"}
[Trust]{.neu-card-title}

- Indexed in MEDLINE, DOAJ, Scopus or Web of Science
- Clear peer-review policy
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#5FA39B"}
[Rules]{.neu-card-title}

- Guide for Authors
- Word limit, checklist
- Registration required?
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0070C0"}
[Cost and speed]{.neu-card-title}

- Article fee (APC) and waivers
- Licence: who may re-use the paper
- Paper 1: 7 weeks. Paper 2: 7 months
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** A good journal is one your readers read, and one that is honestly run.
:::

::: {.notes}
Choose the journal first: its Guide for Authors sets the rules.

Trust: indexed in MEDLINE, DOAJ, Scopus or Web of Science. Cost: the article fee and waivers.

Paper 1 took 7 weeks to acceptance, Paper 2 7 months.

Ask: name one journal your unit reads.
:::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** If a journal finds you by flattering e-mail, check it twice.
:::

::: {.notes}
Predatory journals take fees without real peer review or indexing.

Walk the five red flags on the invented e-mail. Checks: Think.Check.Submit, DOAJ, the NLM Catalog, the hospital librarian.

Poll: did you get an e-mail like this last month?
:::

::: {.neu-banner style="--c:#B5651D"}
LIVE DEMO · 3 min
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}
::: {.neu-activity-steps style="--c:#B5651D"}
- Open the EQUATOR Network website and search 'CONSORT'
- Show the checklist and the flow diagram (Paper 1 has one)
- Find STROBE the same way (Paper 2 and FLUID-ICU)
- Check a journal in DOAJ and in the NLM Catalog
- Open the Think.Check.Submit checklist
:::
:::
::: {.column width="40%"}
::: {.neu-side .plain style="--c:#B5651D"}
Watch for

- Where the checklist PDF is
- How to see if a journal is in MEDLINE
- Three questions to ask any journal
:::
:::
::::

**OUTPUT** Everyone checks the journal and guideline in their own publication plan at home
:::

Demo (20:36-20:39). Script and offline fallback: s8\_demo.md.

EQUATOR: CONSORT, then STROBE. DOAJ, then the NLM Catalog ('currently indexed in MEDLINE'). End on Think.Check.Submit. Paste the four addresses in the chat.

::: {.notes}
The picture groups the nine items of a submission in three columns. The paper: the manuscript, its tables and figures, and the supplementary files (extra tables and figures go here, next to the main ones). The authors and the study: title page, declarations, registration number. For the editor: cover letter, reporting checklist, suggested reviewers.

Journals check the package before any scientific review. Missing items send the paper back.

ORCID iD: a free, permanent researcher identifier. Register at orcid.org.

Paper 1 has a complete declarations block. Template: Cover\_Letter\_Template.

Ask: who already has an ORCID iD?
:::

:::

::: {.notes}
The picture shows six stations from left to right, each with an icon. The orange loop is the revision cycle. The red dashed arrows are the two exits to rejection: at the editor and at the decision. Bottom right: how long our two papers took.

Submit, editor screen (desk rejection is common), 2 or 3 reviewers, decision, revision, acceptance.

One journal at a time. After rejection, improve the paper and submit elsewhere.

Ask: a reviewer is wrong. What do you do? Expected: thank, explain with evidence, clarify the text.
:::

## Check: true or false?

::: {.neu-banner style="--c:#6C3483"}
QUICK QUIZ · 2 min
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}
::: {.neu-activity-steps style="--c:#6C3483"}
- 'A journal that e-mails me first is probably predatory'
- 'I can send my paper to two journals at once to save time'
- 'A preprint has been peer reviewed'
- 'I must answer every reviewer comment, even if I disagree'
- 'The FLUID-ICU paper should follow CONSORT'
:::
:::
::: {.column width="40%"}
::: {.neu-side .plain style="--c:#6C3483"}
Choose

- True
- False
:::
:::
::::

::: {.neu-output style="--c:#6C3483"}
**OUTPUT** Work alone (1 min): mark each statement true or false, then vote in the poll
:::

::: {.notes}
Check (20:48-20:50). 1 minute alone, then one true/false poll each. Call on one or two people to explain statement 1. Answers on the next slide.
:::

## Answers: true or false?

| Statement | Answer | Why |
|:---|:---|:---|
| A journal that e-mails me first is probably predatory | Often true | Many predatory journals write first, so check it twice |
| I can send my paper to two journals at once | False | That is duplicate submission |
| A preprint has been peer reviewed | False | A preprint is posted before peer review |
| I must answer every reviewer comment | True | Answer every point, politely and with evidence |
| The FLUID-ICU paper should follow CONSORT | False | FLUID-ICU is a cohort, so it follows STROBE |

::: {.notes}
Statement 1: an e-mail invitation is a warning sign, not proof. Check the journal before you reply.

Timing: within the 2 minutes of the check.
:::

## Two papers, one question

::: {.neu-intro}
Same clinical question (fluids in septic shock), two designs. Both PDFs were sent by email.
:::

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:2"}
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0D7377"}
[Paper 1: randomised trial]{.neu-card-title}

- Boulet 2024, Critical Care
- Pilot trial, 48 patients analysed
- Restrictive vs usual fluids in septic shock
- Primary outcome: fluid balance on day 5
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0B376C"}
[Paper 2: cohort study]{.neu-card-title}

- Hyun 2023, Annals of Intensive Care
- Propensity-matched cohort, 2516 patients
- Positive fluid balance in sepsis
- Outcome: 28-day mortality
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Same question, two designs: compare what each may claim.
:::

::: {.notes}
Set-up (1 minute): same clinical question, two designs, the same 10 questions.

Paper 1: a pilot trial of 48 patients, with fluid balance on day 5 as the outcome. Paper 2: a matched cohort of 2516 patients, with 28-day mortality as the outcome.

Ask everyone to open both PDFs now.
:::

## The 10-question checklist (1-5)

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:5"}
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0D7377"}
[1  Question]{.neu-card-title}

- Can you write the study's PICO in one line?
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0B376C"}
[2  Design]{.neu-card-title}

- What is the design, and is it the right one for the question?
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#5FA39B"}
[3  Participants]{.neu-card-title}

- Who was included, and who was left out?
- Would your patients have been included?
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0070C0"}
[4  Comparison groups]{.neu-card-title}

- Were the groups similar at the start (Table 1)?
- How was this achieved: randomisation, matching or adjustment?
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#055F56"}
[5  Bias]{.neu-card-title}

- Who knew which group patients were in (blinding)?
- Could that change the outcome?
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Read each question once. Do not give answers.

Q3 is external validity: would your patients be in this study? Q4: look at Table 1.
:::

## The 10-question checklist (6-10)

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:5"}
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0D7377"}
[6  Outcome]{.neu-card-title}

- Was there one pre-specified primary outcome, measured the same way in both groups?
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0B376C"}
[7  Numbers]{.neu-card-title}

- What is the main result as an effect size with 95% CI?
- Is the CI narrow or wide?
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#5FA39B"}
[8  Words vs design]{.neu-card-title}

- Do the conclusions match the design ('associated' vs 'caused', no 'trend' for p = 0.42)?
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0070C0"}
[9  Limitations]{.neu-card-title}

- Are the main limitations stated honestly?
- Name one the authors missed.
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#055F56"}
[10  Use]{.neu-card-title}

- Would this change practice in your unit?
- Why, or why not?
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Q6 and Q7 use Session 6. Q8 is the heart of today: are the words as strong as the design allows? Q9: one limitation the authors missed. Q10: a reason is needed.
:::

After the session, share the class answer grid as a PDF.

**KEY MESSAGE** Randomisation earns the word 'caused'. Observation earns 'associated'.
:::

::: {.notes}
The picture shows two panels, Paper 1 in teal and Paper 2 in blue: how the groups were formed, the main result, what the paper may say (green) and what it may not say (red).

Plenary (21:23-21:28).

Paper 1: randomised, may say 'did not reduce', but 48 patients: no evidence of an effect, not evidence of none, and no 'trend'.

Paper 2: doctors decided the fluid, so 'is associated with', not 'impact'.

Poll: which paper is stronger for causation, which for real-world risk?
:::

## The two papers side by side

| Paper 1: RCT (Boulet 2024) | Paper 2: cohort (Hyun 2023) |
|:---|:---|
| Groups made similar by | Randomisation 1:1 (blocks of 2) | Propensity matching (measured factors only) |
| Who knew the group | Clinicians knew, patients, statistician blinded | Everyone (observational) |
| Main result | 13.2 ml/kg (95% CI -15.2 to 41.6), p = 0.42 | Day 2: HR 2.13 (1.48 to 3.06) |
| Missed limitation | Blocks of 2 with unblinded clinicians | Survivor bias (ICU stay of 3+ days) |
| Wording problem | 'Non-significant trend' (p = 0.42) | 'Impact', 'did not impact', 'show' |
| May claim | Did not reduce day-5 balance (small pilot) | Positive balance associated with death |

::: {.neu-table-caption}
RCT = randomised controlled trial. Pages and details: the trainers' appraisal guide
:::

::: {.notes}
Reveal this table only after the class has answered.

Three messages: design sets the verb, a wide CI means 'we don't know yet', and published is not the same as correct.

Transition: 'You will use the same skills on a classmate's Results section. Here is what your report should look like.'
:::

::: {.notes}
The picture shows the five parts of the review report from Peer\_Review\_Instructions (coloured labels) and, beside each, a short example for a FLUID-ICU Q1 Results draft.

Summary: what the draft found, in your own words, with the main numbers. Strengths: two genuine ones. Major comments: problems that change the numbers or the reader's trust, each with page and line, the problem and a suggestion. Minor comments: wording and format. Recommendation: accept, minor revision or major revision. Attach the completed Results checklist.

Tone: comment on the text, not the person ('the draft gives only the adjusted OR', not 'you forgot'). Ask only for results that are in the author's pack. Never paste a classmate's draft into an AI tool.

Timing (21:28-21:30): 2 minutes. The report is due on Wednesday 30 December, by email to the author and the instructor.
:::

## Key words of Session 8

| Term | In plain words |
|:---|:---|
| Introduction funnel | Known, not known, aim: three paragraphs |
| Six moves | Answer, compare, explain, limitations, implications, conclusion |
| Calibrated language | Verbs as strong as the design allows ('associated', not 'caused') |
| Predatory journal | Takes fees without real peer review or indexing |
| Point-by-point response | A table answering every reviewer comment with the change made |
| Preprint | Public manuscript posted before peer review |

## Preprints, open access and licences

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:3"}
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0D7377"}
[Preprint]{.neu-card-title}

- Posted before peer review (e.g. medRxiv)
- Fast, timestamped, open feedback
- Not peer-reviewed: say so
- Check the journal's policy
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0B376C"}
[Open access]{.neu-card-title}

- Free for everyone to read
- Gold: the journal charges a fee (APC)
- Green: accepted version in a repository
- Ask about fee waivers
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#5FA39B"}
[Licence]{.neu-card-title}

- CC BY: re-use with credit (Paper 2)
- CC BY-NC-ND: share, no changes (Paper 1)
- Read it before you sign
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Know who can read, re-use and pay before you submit.
:::

::: {.notes}
Extra. A preprint is posted before peer review: say so. Gold open access usually has a fee, green means a repository copy. Paper 2 is CC BY, Paper 1 CC BY-NC-ND.
:::

## Rejected? Resubmit smarter

::: {.neu-intro}
Rejection is normal: most papers are rejected at least once.
:::

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:3"}
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0D7377"}
[Desk rejection]{.neu-card-title}

- Out of scope or poorly reported
- Often within days
- Re-target the journal
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0B376C"}
[After review]{.neu-card-title}

- Read the reviews, wait a day
- Fix what they found
- Never resubmit unchanged
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#5FA39B"}
[Next journal]{.neu-card-title}

- Reformat to its Guide for Authors
- Use transfer offers if given
- Appeal only for a clear error
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** The next reviewer may be the same person. Fix the problems first.
:::

::: {.notes}
Extra. Rejection is normal. Desk rejection: re-target. After review: fix what the reviewers found before resubmitting. Never submit to two journals at once.
:::
